title: The brothers' songs
hook: poems of the first monks: forests, rain, freedom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona, who came to the order late and found her strength there. Your line was strength in old age. Did you do one hard thing? Today, the songs turn from the sisters to the brothers. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

Rain on a thatched roof. A peacock calling somewhere in the trees. A man sitting alone in a forest, saying out loud that he is free. These aren't scenes from a novel. They're lines from poems that Buddhist tradition gives to the early monks themselves. Lately we've been listening to the sisters' songs, the Therigatha. It has a companion, a book of the brothers' songs, and today we open it. Today's word is its name.
screen: `RAIN ON A THATCHED ROOF.` → `THE SISTERS' BOOK HAS A COMPANION.` → `TODAY WE OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Theragatha. A thera is an elder, a senior monk, and a gatha is a verse. Verses of the elders. Second, the voice. Each poem carries a monk's name, and tradition says the monk himself spoke it, often about the moment he was freed, or looking back on the road there. So these aren't sermons about the monks. They're his own words, in the first person: I went to the forest, I sat, I was set free. Third, what they sing about. Forests. Caves and rocky hills. Clouds and rain. Animals: peacocks, elephants, cranes. And again and again, freedom: the work is done, the burden is down, there is nothing more to do. Some poems are a single verse. Some run on for pages, and in one of them a monk argues with his own mind. Fourth, how to read them. Some readers find them strangely close to us: a man in a hut, listening to the rain, and glad. Others notice how much they repeat: the same phrases close poem after poem, almost like a chorus. Both are there: a shared chorus, and one person's afternoon of rain and peacocks. The brothers' book sits beside the sisters' book among the short texts of the Pali canon. Over the coming days we'll meet some of these brothers by name: a monk with a dry roof, a man who swept away old flowers, a former bandit, an actor, the great disciples. Each one, in his own words.
screen: `THERA, AN ELDER. GATHA, A VERSE.` · `EACH POEM CARRIES A MONK'S NAME.` · `FORESTS, RAIN AND FREEDOM.` · `A CHORUS, AND ONE MAN'S AFTERNOON.` · then, large: `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one short poem. Any poem will do, from an old book or a new one, or one you've known by heart since school. Read it slowly, once, out loud if you can. Then put it down and sit. Let one line stay with you. Not its meaning, just its sound, or its picture: rain, a hill, a bird. When the mind wanders off, come back to that one line, the way you'd come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Theragatha. The verses of the elders: songs the tradition gives to the early monks, spoken in their own voices. Today's word.
Your line: his own words. Today, when someone tells you something in their own words, not a report about it, listen a little longer than usual. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: In Theravada communities, verses from the Theragatha are read and taught alongside the Therigatha, and teachers often draw on single poems from it as short reflections.
